A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same low-rank refusal-vector work and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. The original derivation, qualitative figures, and prompt lists can be matched across restructuring. Internal reporting inconsistencies do not prevent a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original Open-Sora censorship, FVD, and MM-Notox results on T2VSafetyBench, qualitative generations, and rank and suppression-strength experiments in Section 4.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds ZeroScopeT2V/SafeSora evaluations, competing methods, component analyses, multi-concept experiments, and adversarial testing in the main text and appendices.

M1.justification: The core activation-difference averaging, cPCA refinement, and closed-form weight update remain. Appendix C.3 adds a multi-concept extension using several refusal directions, concept-specific suppression strengths, and sequential application; v1 explicitly restricted the method to one concept at a time.

E1.justification: T2VSafetyBench coverage is retained, while SafeSora adds evaluated content including terrorism, racism, and animal abuse. v2 also introduces joint multi-category removal and targeted adversarial-prompt scenarios, substantially broadening the tested requirements and input conditions.

E2.justification: v1 compares the edited model with unmodified Open-Sora. v2 adds NullSCE to the T2VSafetyBench comparison, SAFREE to SafeSora, and an adapted UCE comparison in Appendix F. NullSCE has no Gore entry in Table 1; VideoEraser remains related work rather than an evaluated comparator.

E3.justification: The reported evaluator changes from GPT-4 to GPT-4o. FVD changes from XCLIP features and original-versus-censored comparisons to I3D features with real-video references; MM-Notox's printed definition also changes. v2 adds ZeroScopeT2V, FVMD, and new experimental protocols, including attacks on 100 previously fully censored prompts. The stated selected layers change from 17–19 to 17–18. These are reported setting changes, not proof that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The original rank and suppression-strength studies remain. v2 adds safe/unsafe-pair similarity tests, neutral-set resampling, refusal-only versus PCA versus cPCA comparisons, alpha sensitivity, multi-vector interference and quality analysis, UCE hyperparameter sweeps, and targeted adversarial testing. These directly examine component necessity, sensitivity, and failure conditions.

E5.justification: v2 Table 4 newly reports five random neutral-set resamplings and their individual censorship rates, providing limited variability evidence absent from v1. This does not establish increased repeated runs for the main benchmarks. Neither version provides general benchmark confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: The five original Open-Sora censorship pairs remain unchanged, but FVD and MM-Notox entries are replaced: for example, censored Pornography FVD changes from 144.0 to 151.24 and MM-Notox from 20.89 to 20.07. Revised metric definitions prevent interpreting these as same-setting performance changes. v2 adds substantial comparator, SafeSora, FVMD, sensitivity, multi-vector, and attack results.

T1.justification: The main projection mathematics and Appendix B weight-update derivation are retained. Appendix C.3 adds a mathematical multi-concept extension summing projections across refusal directions. Equation 10 also changes the defined MM-Notox distance from an L2 norm to a squared norm. No substantial new proof framework is introduced.

C1.justification: The broad first-video-unlearning positioning becomes a specific first training-free, closed-form weight-update claim, accompanied by explicit superiority claims over competing video methods. v2 also claims irreversible weight-level changes in its introduction, whereas v1 explicitly acknowledged adversarial reversibility. These revise novelty, comparative effectiveness, and protection claims.

C2.justification: v1's explicit misuse, governance, and vector-reversal limitations disappear. v2 adds substantive interpretations of prompt-selection stability, cPCA's benefits, neutral-concept overlap, UCE's fidelity tradeoff, and adversarial resistance. Appendix C.3 newly identifies substantial quality degradation when five vectors affect complex motion, extending the discussion of applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 adds ZeroScopeT2V injection locations, approximately 1,000 GPT-sampled neutral prompts, UCE retain-prompt lists and scales, and computational estimates including 0.4 GPU hours and ten forward passes. The detailed v1 layer-sweep rationale is removed. Original example prompt lists, project-page information, and code-folder availability statements are retained.

R1.justification: v2 substantially revises positioning around SAFREE, VideoEraser, and NullSCE, distinguishing filtering, fine-tuning, and training-free weight updates rather than asserting an unaddressed video-unlearning field. It also adds relevant benchmark, metric, model-editing, and attack references. The duplicated ModelScope entries represent the same previously cited work.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and substantial method and evaluation passages are rewritten. Section 4.4 becomes an expanded Section 5 Discussion, the standalone Limitations section disappears, and new appendix sections surround retained qualitative material and prompt lists. This is extensive narrative restructuring beyond adding experiments.

P2.justification: The original results displays are reorganized into grouped comparison tables with censorship, FVD, MM-Notox, and averages, followed by numerous new analysis tables. Figure 1 moves to the first page and Figure 2 becomes a compact grid. ICLR formatting changes typography and placement throughout; the underlying images in Figures 1–12 are retained.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked competing unlearning baselines and direct controls establishing cPCA's contribution. v2 substantially addresses these deficiencies through comparative evaluations, a second model and benchmark, component controls, and tests exposing multi-concept and adversarial behavior. These gains outweigh the loss of explicit limitations and reporting problems, including the mismatched-category NullSCE average and inconsistent UCE dataset label. The broader evidence improves assessment of effectiveness and boundaries, although it does not establish the claimed irreversibility.
